lead: In English tradition this day has long been called Spy Wednesday, for the Gospel in which Judas goes to the chief priests. Isaiah’s Servant and Matthew’s Judas stand as opposites. The Servant’s ear is opened every morning, and he turns neither back nor aside. Judas hears the same Teacher every day, and looks for his opportunity. Psalm 69, which the New Testament often quotes of the Passion, prays between them: “Insults have broken my heart”.

set: This is the third Servant Song. The word “servant” does not appear in the song itself but in the verse just after it (50:10). Here for the first time we hear plainly of suffering. The speaker is a disciple who is beaten for what he has been given to say, yet he remains sure of God’s help. Part of this reading was also heard on Palm Sunday, as the first reading before the Passion. Today we hear it as far as the question “who will declare me guilty?”
str: vv. 4–5a: the disciple’s tongue and ear.
vv. 5b–6: he does not resist: back, cheeks, face.
vv. 7–9a: God helps him; he faces his accusers as if in court.
kw: The Hebrew word comes twice in v. 4. A teacher is first of all one who is taught: the word that comforts comes from an ear that has listened.
The Hebrew repeats the word. This is not one great vision but a daily schooling, the prayer of an ordinary morning repeated.

One of the hardest stones of the region. “I have set my face like flint” is not hardness toward others, but a firmness that does not turn back. Luke says that Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51).
vv: The Lord God has given me the tongue of a teacher, that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word.
The purpose of this gift is the tired person in front of us.
I gave my back to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who pulled out the beard; I did not hide my face from insult and spitting.

To pull out a man’s beard was a deep humiliation in that world. The Gospels recall the blows and the spitting at the trial of Jesus (Matthew 26:67; 27:30). The verbs are active: he gave his back. Suffering is not simply something that befalls him.
he who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me?
St Paul takes up the language of this courtroom in Romans 8:33–34: “It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn?”
ch: The Church reads this song of Christ, of whom Peter writes, “When he was abused, he did not return abuse” (1 Peter 2:23), and the Catechism counts it among the Songs that proclaim the meaning of his Passion (CCC 713). Anyone who teaches the faith can make v. 4 a morning prayer. It gives the order of a Christian day: first to listen, then to speak.

set: Matthew has just told of the woman who anointed Jesus at Bethany (26:6–13), and now he sets another disciple’s act beside it. She gives away something costly for him. Judas asks what he can get for him. The scene then moves to the preparation for the Passover and the meal itself.
str: vv. 14–16: Judas and the chief priests.
vv. 20–25: at table: “one of you will betray me”.
kw: The key verb of the Passion, here in vv. 15, 16, 21, 23, 24 and 25. It can also mean simply to hand over. People hand Jesus over; yet behind them, as Paul says, God “gave him up for all of us” (Romans 8:32, the same verb).

Only Matthew gives the sum. It recalls the price for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32) and the shepherd’s insulting wage in Zechariah 11:12–13, which Matthew takes up in 27:9–10. A small price for such a man.

The word means a set, decisive time. The disciples are told to say it to a stranger in the city. Judas is watching for an opportunity (v. 16, eukairia, from the same root), but the true time belongs to Jesus.
vv: “What will you give me if I betray him to you?”

Only Matthew has Judas ask this, which fits the charge of greed in John 12:6. Why he really did it the Gospels do not fully explain. This passage names some of the chief priests, not the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
And they became greatly distressed and began to say to him one after another, “Surely not I, Lord?”
The Greek form expects the answer “no”, yet they ask, and none is sure of himself. It is a healthy fear.
Judas, who betrayed him, said, “Surely not I, Rabbi?” He replied, “You have said so.”
The others say “Lord”; Judas says “Rabbi”, a title Jesus had told his disciples not to claim (23:8). The answer leaves the responsibility with the one who asks. Even now, there is still time.
ch: The Church has never taught that God made Judas betray: God “predestines no one to go to hell” (CCC 1037). Verse 24 joins two truths: “as it is written” means that God’s plan is not defeated, and “woe” means that the human act remains guilty. The Mass, too, is set in this story: Paul begins his account of it with “on the night when he was betrayed” (1 Corinthians 11:23). We approach the table knowing that we might be the one who asks, “Surely not I?”

qa: Does “better not to have been born” mean that Judas is in hell?

The words are a grave warning, and Christian writers have often been severe about Judas. But the Church has never declared of any named person that he is lost, and she leaves the judgment to God. What we must take from the verse is the seriousness of sin, and our own need of mercy.
study: What is my “morning by morning”? When and how does God open my ear each day?
Judas asked, “What will you give me?” Where in my life am I tempted to set a price on my fidelity?
